task_statement:
Research question (as posed on 2026-06-19, in the area of play-type labeling and data quality):
Opponent next-possession PPP after you run play X is large enough to drive AVOID labels; own-sequence lags similarly matter.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

research_concepts: AVOID labeling (lowest-ranked counter play type after a suppression trigger)
methodological_questions: How to define the boundary of the next opponent possession when free throws, end-of-period events, or jump balls intervene.
What magnitude of opponent next-possession PPP difference is considered 'large enough' to drive an AVOID label.
Whether AVOID labels from the strategy app are derived from outcomes that include future possessions, creating look-ahead bias.
How to disentangle the effect of the preceding play type from the influence of the possession outcome (made shot, missed shot, turnover) and game situation.
Whether sample sizes of conditional opponent possessions per play type are sufficient for reliable inference.
How to control for team defensive quality and opponent strength when measuring opponent next-possession PPP.
How to define own-sequence lags (immediately after the opponent's reply, or multiple lags) and their role.
evidence_does_not_establish: No prior project records on this exact question were retrieved, so no historical evidence exists to establish or refute any part of it.
own_inferences: Opponent next-possession PPP and own-sequence lags can be computed from the available per-game play-by-play data, but careful parsing rules are needed to handle free throws, end-of-period, and technical fouls to avoid misalignment.

The AVOID label system described in the glossary uses within-game H1-to-H2 PPP drops and matchup-ranked counters; it does not explicitly use opponent next-possession outcomes. Whether those outcomes are 'large enough to drive AVOID labels' depends on an unspecified threshold for practical significance.
If AVOID labels are based on historical data that overlap with the sample used to compute opponent next-possession PPP, the analysis risks circularity (outcome-derived labels)

The effect of a play type on the opponent's next possession is likely confounded by how the possession ended (e.g., a turnover leads to a live-ball situation that raises opponent PPP mechanically) and by the defensive strength of the team.
Sample sizes for rare play types and for specific team-opponent matchups may be too small to yield stable estimates.
uncertainties: The precise definition of AVOID labels in the project's strategy app and whether they incorporate information from games that post-date the possessions being analyzed.
Whether 'own-sequence lags' means the team's very next possession after the opponent's reply or a longer lag structure.
The threshold for what constitutes a large enough difference in opponent next-possession PPP to influence AVOID labelling (the research question provides no quantitative anchor).
The handling of possessions that end in free throws where the opponent's next possession starts after the last free throw.
Whether the strategy app's AVOID labels are specific to a matchup or general, and whether they are generated at the possession level or at the game/season level.

historical_effect.explanation: No historical records were available, so the assessment rests entirely on the research question, the available data, and methodological reasoning.

blocking_constraints.text: No agreed operational definition of 'next possession' when free throws, end-of-quarter, or technical fouls intervene; any choice will affect measured opponent PPP.
The AVOID labels likely derive from data that may overlap with the test sample; using the same games to compute opponent next-possession PPP and AVOID labels could create look-ahead bias.

The type of possession ending (made basket, defensive rebound, live-ball turnover) and the game situation (score margin, time remaining) strongly predict opponent next-possession PPP, confounding the play type's independent effect.

prior_work.summary: No earlier project studies were found that addressed opponent next-possession outcomes or own-sequence lags in relation to AVOID labels.

risks.text: The boundary of the next possession is ambiguous when free throws or end-of-period events intervene; measurement error can bias estimates.
If AVOID labels are computed using the same season's data that also supplies the opponent next-possession outcomes, the analysis suffers from look-ahead bias.

The relationship between a play type and the opponent's subsequent PPP is confounded by how the possession ends (shot make/miss, turnover) and by the team's defensive ability, which cannot be fully controlled.
Some play types occur rarely, and conditioning on the play type while also requiring a clear next opponent possession drastically reduces sample sizes, leading to underpowered tests.
Testing many play types and lags simultaneously without correction inflates the chance of false positives.
If AVOID labels are already derived from possession outcomes, using them as a benchmark risks circular validation.
For many play-type × team × game combinations, the number of opponent next possessions is very small, leading to unstable estimates.
Without a clear threshold for 'large enough', any difference found could be dismissed as too small to matter, or post hoc thresholds could be chosen.

design.estimand: Average opponent points per possession on the possession immediately following a team running play type X, relative to the average opponent PPP after all other play types, controlling for team defensive rating, possession-ending event, and game situation. Secondary estimand: the same team's PPP on its very next offensive possession (own-sequence lag), again relative to baseline.
design.unit: Possession pair: the focal team's offensive possession labeled with a play type, and the immediately subsequent opponent possession (and, separately, the team's next own possession). Only pairs where the next possession can be unambiguously identified after handling free throws and end-of-period are retained.
design.sample: NBA regular-season and playoff games from complete seasons 2022-23, 2023-24, 2024-25, and the complete portion of 2025-26. Exclude garbage time (Q4 or OT with score margin >20). Include only play types with at least 200 occurrences across the sample.
design.power: No formal power calculation is feasible without specifying a minimal effect size of practical interest. The design would be exploratory; a sensitivity analysis would determine the minimum detectable effect given the observed sample sizes per play type.
design.controls: Fixed effects for team (offense), opponent (defense), home/away. Covariates: preceding possession outcome (made FG, missed FG + defensive rebound, live-ball turnover, dead-ball turnover, shooting foul + free throws), score margin (linear and quadratic), seconds remaining in period, period number, offensive and defensive team pre-game opponent-adjusted efficiency ratings.
design.falsification: Shuffle play-type labels within each team-game (preserving possession order) and recompute opponent next-possession PPP differences; the distribution under the null should center near zero. Additionally, test whether the metric is stable across seasons and independent of the AVOID labeling algorithm's training window.
design.multiplicity: Apply Bonferroni-Holm correction across the set of tested play types and lags. Pre-register which play types are of primary interest.
design.decision_rule: The study would not aim to decide whether the observed differences 'are large enough to drive AVOID labels' without a pre-specified policy-relevant threshold. Instead, it would report the estimated differences with confidence intervals and compare the ranking of play types by this metric to the ranking of AVOID labels from a temporally prior season (using only 2022-23 and 2023-24 to compute labels, and 2024-25 as hold-out). The study would conclude that the metric is potentially useful if the worst-ranked play types by opponent next-possession PPP align with AVOID labels significantly more than chance, and the effect size exceeds 0.05 PPP.
design.data_version: NBA stats API per-game files and derived play-type possession graph database as of 2026-06-19.
